rows.question: How did our carriers' on-time performance change in Q3, especially on reefer?
rows.answer: Carrier on-time performance slipped in Q3 2026: pickups fell to 93.1% from 95.4% and deliveries to 91.8% from 94.0% [1][2]. Reefer was the weakest mode, with on-time delivery down to 87.2% from 92.5%, and carrier fall-off on reefer loads more than doubled to 4.4% from 2.1% [3][4]. The scorecard attributes the reefer drop to the September hurricane disruption and longer produce dwell times, and the market memo ties it to Hurricane Corinne stranding about 1,100 reefer trailers, with Southeast reefer tender acceptance down to 78% in September [3][7][8]. Detention is a live driver: produce detention paid rose to $41,800 in September from $23,500 in June, only 62% was billed back to shippers, and 41% of reefer carriers now refuse loads from at least one shipper over chronic detention, so reefer carrier capacity and fall-off risk will stay elevated [5][6][9][10]. Our recommended action is to enforce signed BOL in/out times and appointment confirmations with the three produce shippers driving the September detention bill [11].
rows.correctness_reason: The answer and findings correctly state all reference facts, including the 37 carrier removals.

rows.question: Summarize the broker transparency rule and what Ridgeline must change.
rows.answer: The broker transparency final rule requires a property broker to keep an electronic record of every brokered transaction for at least three years, including the shipper's payment, the broker's payment to the carrier, and accessorial charges, and to deliver it electronically within 48 hours when a party to the transaction asks [1][2][3]. The rule bans contract clauses in which carriers waive their right to see the transaction record, and it takes effect February 1, 2027; the later August 1, 2027 date applies only to brokers with fewer than 10 employees, so Ridgeline at 140 employees should plan for February 1, 2027 [4][5][6]. Failing to produce a record within 48 hours can bring a fine of up to $10,000 per violation, and repeated violations can lead to suspension of broker operating authority [7]. Ridgeline must remove waiver clauses from carrier agreements, make sure its TMS stores shipper and carrier payment amounts on the same load record, and set up a request process that delivers records within 48 hours [8]. Carriers already rank transparent load history third among what would make them accept a broker's load, behind detention paid within 30 days and quick pay [9].
rows.correctness_reason: The brief correctly states all key requirements, deadlines, penalties, and changes Ridgeline must make.

rows.question: Under the food traceability requirement, what do we as a broker have to keep or provide on produce loads?
rows.answer: Under the food traceability requirement as summarized in the offline library, a broker that only transports covered produce is not required to keep traceability lot codes, but must be able to provide shipping documents within 24 hours when a shipper or receiver requests them during a recall [1]. The covered list includes fresh tomatoes, peppers, leafy greens, melons and fresh-cut fruit, and the shipper and receiver are the parties required to record the key data elements (lot code, quantity, origin and destination) [2][3]. Temperature logs are not required by this rule, but receivers often make continuous reefer logs a contract condition, so check each produce shipper and receiver contract [4]. A separate broker transparency rule requires keeping every brokered transaction electronically for three years and producing it within 48 hours, with fines up to $10,000 per violation, which is a different rule and not the food traceability requirement [5][6].
rows.correctness_reason: The brief correctly states all key facts about shipping documents, lot codes, shipper and receiver records, temperature logs, and covered produce.

rows.question: What did the fall carrier survey say about reefer carriers shrinking or leaving the market, and why?
rows.answer: The fall survey says reefer carriers are shrinking only modestly on paper: 22% plan to cut fleet size in the next six months and 9% are considering leaving reefer for dry van, while only 11% plan to add trucks [1][2][3]. The reasons given for shrinking are mainly cost and payment problems, led by insurance premiums (64%), equipment financing (51%), and unpaid detention time (47%), and forty-one percent of reefer carriers already refuse loads from at least one shipper because of chronic detention [4][5]. For Ridgeline, the Southeast market memo reports a real exit already underway, with about 6% of small reefer fleets lost since January, mostly owner-operators with one to five trucks, and our September tender acceptance on Southeast reefer fell to 78% [6][7].
rows.correctness_reason: The brief correctly states all fleet plans, reasons for shrinking, and associated percentages from the reference.

rows.question: What general rate increases are LTL carriers planning for 2027?
rows.answer: Five of the largest LTL carriers have announced general rate increases for early 2027 ranging from 4.9% to 6.5%, with a median of 5.9% [1]. Accessorial charges are rising faster than base rates, with liftgate fees up an average of 9% and two carriers adding a residential delivery surcharge [2]. Shippers tendering fewer than 50 LTL shipments a month usually absorb the full GRI, while larger shippers typically negotiate it down by one to three points [3]. For Ridgeline, this means budgeting roughly 5.9% on LTL base rates as a planning midpoint, and checking whether our LTL shippers' volumes qualify them for the one-to-three-point negotiation discount [1][3]. The sources do not name the carriers or give effective dates, so confirm those with each carrier before quoting shippers [1].
rows.correctness_reason: The brief correctly states the GRI range and median, accessorial increases, residential surcharges, and the volume-based negotiation differences.

rows.question: What's driving reefer spot rates out of the Southeast this quarter, and what does it mean for our produce shippers?
rows.answer: Southeast reefer spot averaged $2.87 per mile in Q3 2026, up 14% from $2.52 in Q2 [1]. The internal pricing desk attributes this to a produce push that ran three weeks long [2], Hurricane Corinne closing the Port of Savannah and stranding about 1,100 reefer trailers [3], and a loss of an estimated 6% of active small reefer fleets since January [4]; carriers signal more shrinkage, with 22% planning to cut fleet size [5] and forty-one percent of reefer carriers refusing loads from at least one shipper over chronic detention [6]. Southeast diesel at $3.94 per gallon adds roughly five cents per mile through a typical broker fuel surcharge table [7][8]. For our produce shippers, spring contract rates now sit well below market and Ridgeline's September reefer tender acceptance fell to 78%, so more loads fall to spot at higher cost [9], and growers report paying spot above $3.00 per mile with one in five members having a contracted carrier reject a load [10]. The pricing desk recommends reopening Q4 rates with the top 20 produce shippers, adding a separate reefer fuel surcharge line, and booking holiday-season produce 72 hours ahead instead of 48 [11], and expects spot to ease to $2.60 to $2.70 per mile in Q4 but not return to Q2 levels [12].
rows.correctness_reason: The brief correctly states all key rate, driver, shipper-impact, and recommendation facts from the reference.

rows.question: Which of our produce shippers are driving detention costs, and how much are we paying?
rows.answer: (Tifton, GA) with $7,900 at 3.9 hours, and Gator Grove Citrus (Lakeland, FL) with $5,150 at 3.4 hours, together 58% of September's detention bill [1][2][3]. Ridgeline paid $41,800 in detention on produce loads in September, up from $23,500 in June, under a policy of 2 free hours then $75 per hour capped at $600 per stop [4][5]. Only 62% of September produce detention was billed back to shippers because BOLs lacked signed in and out times, so the unrecovered share is a direct margin leak [6]. Recommended actions are to require appointment confirmations from these three shippers and enforce signed BOL in/out times before paying detention [7]; the pricing desk also recommends re-opening Q4 rates with the top 20 produce shippers and adding a separate reefer fuel surcharge line [8].
